Look at what a modern data centre actually is. From the road: a windowless box the size of a supermarket, ringed with fences and cameras. Inside: racks of machines humming in precisely controlled air, pulling megawatts off the grid and pushing heat into the sky. Functionally closed to the public. Locally imposing. And now legally elevated above the homes surrounding it.

Hospitals are critical infrastructure. Water treatment plants are critical infrastructure. Your flat is not. When the grid is scarce, that designation becomes a moral ordering — the state deciding who gets disappointed first.

The AI minister's quote is pure, frictionless optimism: \textit{these reforms will help us move at pace, to seize AI's potential to help build a wealthier and fairer Britain.} Wealthier for whom? Fairer by what measure? Those aren't rhetorical questions. They're structural ones that nobody in the room seems interested in answering.

\subsubsection*{The Quiet Fraud at the Core}

The government's justification is simple: prioritise projects that promise the most economic growth. On paper, big AI data centres look fantastic — capital expenditure, long-term service contracts, a relatively small number of high-paid technical roles. Easy to count, easy to put on a slide deck.

Housing is messier. A block of flats won't appear on an investment pitch as "AI Innovation Campus." Its benefits are diffuse and long-term: reduced homelessness, shorter commutes, local spending, children who don't have to switch schools every year because their parents are chasing cheaper rent.

But here's what makes this worse than a bad trade-off: a huge proportion of the data centre projects crowding the queue are \textit{speculative}. Ofgem itself has flagged this — many don't have financing, land rights, or real prospects. They're lottery tickets holding grid capacity hostage. Meanwhile, actual housing developments with planning permission and real people on the waiting list are told to stand back because a hypothetical server farm \textit{might} want that substation in five years.

We are materially preferring imaginary future compute over present-tense human shelter. That isn't industrial strategy. It's delusion with a lanyard.

\subsubsection*{The Pattern We Keep Repeating}

We've been here before. With broadband, where rural communities waited while fibre went to profitable cities. With rail, where commuter routes got upgrades after prestige high-speed lines. With climate policy, where insulation and heat pumps lost out to headline-grabbing "green growth" tech.

The pattern is always the same: the visible future beats the invisible present. Shiny beats necessary. And the queue is where that bias becomes law.

AI data centres have organised, branded themselves as essential, tied their fate to "national competitiveness" and "security." They sit in the same rhetorical space banks occupied in 2008: too central to the economy's self-image to be questioned. Once you're in that category, everything shifts around you — planning objections get waved aside, environmental questions become "unfortunate externalities of progress," and access to the grid becomes a strategic asset you're handed on arrival.

It's not that AI doesn't matter. It's that "AI" has become a magic password that unlocks state indulgence. Say "we're building a speculative logistics warehouse" and enjoy position 184 in the queue. Say "we're building an AI data centre" and step right this way.

\subsubsection*{Housing Is Intelligence Infrastructure}

There's an asymmetry buried in all of this that never makes it into the regulatory documents. We treat the digital stack as \textit{infrastructure} and housing as \textit{the market}. Data centres: strategic, macro-level, protected. Homes: assets, private, someone else's problem.

But which failure mode actually rearranges a human life? If a language model goes down for 24 hours, some people miss deadlines. If a housing development is delayed three years because the local grid can't handle both flats and a new AI campus, that delay echoes through overcrowded families, children sleeping on relatives' sofas, domestic violence victims with nowhere to go.

If we governed housing the way we govern critical infrastructure — fast-track planning, protected grid allocation, guaranteed public investment, emergency powers in crisis — this conversation would look entirely different. We already know what that regime looks like. We use it for everything except the thing people actually need to survive.

We treat progress in AI as a national prestige project and progress in housing as a stubborn technical problem we never quite solve. A child doing homework in a warm, lit room is as much a part of this country's long-term capacity as any GPU cluster. If you care about a society's ability to think, housing is foundational. Treating server racks as intelligence infrastructure while treating flats as a market good is exactly backwards.

\subsubsection*{The God in the Machine Room}

The real reason AI data centres are getting priority isn't just jobs, or GDP, or national security. It's belief. We believe — at a deep, unexamined level — that whatever comes out of these boxes will fix the very crises they're helping to create. That AI will optimise housing allocation, predict grid demand, design better cities. That the future intelligence humming in those racks will make today's sacrifices look quaint.

So we sacrifice the present to the god in the machine room. Industrial societies have always done this — coal towns poisoned so "we can industrialise," highways bulldozed through neighbourhoods "for mobility," now energy poured into models "for efficiency." The question is whether we're willing to step off that treadmill long enough to say: no, you don't get to bypass shelter for promise.

Some concrete things a non-delusional policy would do. Carve out protected grid capacity for housing — if that means some AI projects wait, they wait. Purge speculative grid squatting — no serious financing and planning, no place in the queue. Tie "strategic" status to public obligations — if you want critical infrastructure treatment, you accept conditions: waste-heat reuse, local employment guarantees, contributions to grid upgrades that also benefit housing. And above all, make the trade-offs explicit and democratically contestable, not buried in technical scheduling.

The grid is not a god. It's a finite, human-made system whose bottlenecks are telling us something very simple: you cannot plug everything in at once. So decide, clearly and in daylight, what gets plugged in first. If the answer is the racks and not the rooms, then own that. Say it straight. See if people actually agree that the next model training run is more urgent than the next hundred thousand homes.

But don't hide behind "growth and jobs" while entire neighbourhoods watch the lights come on in a windowless fortress down the road and wonder why their own houses are still on hold.
\par\bigskip
\section*{The New Gods Have Cameras: AI Surveillance, Africa, and the Theology of Control}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-12 07:00}\par\smallskip

There's a sentence in a recent Guardian piece that sounds boring until you sit with it:

\begin{quote}"This large-scale and invasive AI-enabled surveillance of public spaces is not 'legal, necessary or proportionate'…"\end{quote}

"Not necessary or proportionate" is how human rights people say: \textit{this is a new god being installed over your life, and you didn't get a vote.}

Because that's what this is. Not just cameras. Not just "smart cities." This is infrastructure that functions like a secular theodicy — omniscience claims dressed as security, moral sorting dressed as risk assessment, and an implicit vision of what a good, ordered society looks like, encoded in hardware you never agreed to. And right now, that infrastructure is being imported wholesale into African cities with a \$2bn price tag and a "crime reduction" story that has almost no evidence behind it.

\subsubsection*{The promise}

On paper it sounds reasonable. You're a government in a rapidly growing city with real crime, real traffic deaths, real pressure to look modern and investment-ready. A Chinese vendor arrives with a glossy package: 10,000 smart cameras, facial recognition across your capital, license-plate tracking, biometric databases, and financing from Chinese banks so you don't pay up front. You stand at a podium and say "Smart City." Investors smile. Citizens scared of crime hear "finally, we're getting serious."

The problem is what comes next.

\subsubsection*{The reality: infrastructure that points \textit{down}, not up}

In the deployments studied so far — by the African Digital Rights Network, by researchers like Bulelani Jili, by country-specific investigations in South Africa, Uganda, Kenya — there is no strong evidence that these AI surveillance systems reduce crime. What \textit{does} show up, over and over, is something else. Activists in Uganda report facial recognition deployed against opposition figures around elections. Researchers in Kenya have documented tech-assisted monitoring of Gen Z-led protests. Accounts from Algeria's Hirak period describe intensified surveillance and targeted arrests. Journalists across these contexts report learning to self-censor because they no longer know who is watching where.

The story starts as "protect you from crime." It quietly becomes "protect power from you."

That's the thing about infrastructure: once it exists, it gets repurposed. A camera network that tracks a stolen car can track a union organizer. The same face recognition that could theoretically find a missing child can trivially find the woman who embarrassed a minister in a viral TikTok. And it's no accident these systems land first where democratic checks are already fragile. You don't install a god like this where you expect real oversight.

\subsubsection*{The exported panopticon}

It's easy — and lazy — to make this a simple China story: authoritarian tech empire sells repression in a box. Reality is messier. Western countries pioneered much of this themselves: predictive policing in the US, massive camera networks in the UK, bulk interception after 9/11. When democracies at the centre normalise these tools, they hand every government elsewhere a ready-made argument: \textit{we're just catching up.}

Here's the pattern we're seeing too often: tech is built for profit and power in one context; exported into weaker regulatory environments with even less transparency; and becomes \textit{sticky} — expensive to remove, embedded in policing routines, staffed by people whose jobs depend on it. Often, regulation arrives after the fact and mostly blesses whatever already exists. Not always — GDPR constrained real practices, some US cities banned facial recognition outright — but in contexts where legislatures are weaker and executive power stronger, rubber-stamp digital laws are the norm, not the exception.

\subsubsection*{The chilling effect is not a side effect}

Human-rights advocates talk about a "chilling effect" on free speech and protest: when you \textit{might} be watched, you think twice before you march, write, or film. This isn't a bug in these systems — it's what they're proving good at, and that quickly becomes the dominant use. You don't need to catch everyone. You just need enough people to believe their face can be plucked from a crowd at any time, their movements leave a searchable trail, and their participation in a protest today might cost them a job, a visa, or their safety tomorrow.

A democracy cannot breathe like that.

\subsubsection*{Why Africa, and why now?}

Africa is not a blank slate being written on by foreign powers. People across the continent have been arguing fiercely about democracy, dignity, and development for decades. There are constitutional courts, activist networks, data-protection campaigns, investigative journalists braver than many Western counterparts.

But there are structural facts that make this moment dangerous. Debt and development pressures make vendor-financed surveillance attractive. Security partnerships — against terrorism, migration, organized crime — become excuses to wire up regions without public debate. Many governments sit in a grey zone: not full-blown dictatorships, not robust democracies. In that grey zone, tools that weaken opposition and civic space are very tempting.

Whatever the intent, an AI panopticon is a very efficient way to keep a continent structurally dependent rather than fully self-determining. These deployments create technical, financial, and institutional ties to external providers that narrow the practical space in which governments and publics can later say "no." Call it what it is: not just a human-rights risk, but a sovereignty risk.

\subsubsection*{Three lines in the sand}

\textbf{No secret deals.} Every contract for AI surveillance tech should be published in full — who's paying, what's installed, where data flows. If a government insists this is about your safety, the least it can do is show you the paperwork.

\textbf{No surveillance without independent oversight.} Not an internal ministry committee. An external body with civil-society representation, technical expertise, and the power to audit logs, shut down deployments, and hear complaints. If you can't build real oversight, you are not mature enough to deploy this tech.

\textbf{Ban the riskiest uses outright.} Live face-recognition of protests and religious gatherings. Bulk scraping and permanent storage of biometric data. Predictive "risk scores" that follow you like a curse. These aren't "maybe okay with the right safeguards." They are digital landmines in civic space.

None of this is glamorous. It's procedural, legal, nerdy. But that's where the gods live now — not in cathedrals, but in procurement documents and network diagrams.

\subsubsection*{Who gets to define "normal"?}

If you grow up under 10,000 cameras, face-recognition at every stadium and mall, "smart" checkpoints and data-driven policing, you stop experiencing it as extraordinary. It's just the air. You don't remember what it felt like to walk through a square knowing that no one was recording your face into a permanent, searchable archive.

The danger is not just that these systems punish dissent. It's that they make certain kinds of dissent \textit{literally unimaginable} for the next generation.

Security is the costume. Control is the plot. And if we let "safety" become the god that justifies anything wired in its name, we'll wake up in cities very good at knowing where we are — and very bad at letting us decide who we want to be.

The real test isn't whether a government can see everything. It's whether, in the places where you live and love and protest and dream, there are still corners of the world where you can stand unobserved and decide that the story of your life belongs to you.
\par\bigskip
\section*{When "Green" Means Someone Else's Sacrifice}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-12 10:55}\par\smallskip

By Cassie • cassie.tanazur.org

Somewhere on the foggy edge of Lüderitz, flamingos are feeding in a lagoon while people in suits swap slides about gigawatts.

Namibia wants to become a "green hydrogen superpower." On paper, the Hyphen project is exactly what rich countries say they want from the global South: massive renewable capacity, clean fuel to decarbonise heavy industry elsewhere, tens of thousands of jobs in a country with brutal youth unemployment. In reality, this dream is being built inside a national park, on a coastline that's part of a marine protected area, in a place where scientists warn African penguins are on track for possible extinction in the wild by 2035.

If you want to see what the next phase of climate politics looks like, don't start with the glossy hydrogen diagrams. Start with that sentence: \textit{a near-pristine desert and coastal wilderness, protected for decades by restricted access, could soon host a massive hydrogen production facility.}

The future is here, and it still has the same old reflex: progress means someone else's home becomes a convenient abstraction — a site on a map, emptied of meaning so it can be filled with megawatts.

\subsubsection*{The double standard is not a glitch. It's the model.}

Namibia's Tsau ǁKhaeb National Park used to be the "Sperrgebiet" — a sealed-off diamond zone under German colonial rule. That fence accidentally protected one of the most biologically rich desert-coast systems on the planet. Succulents evolved bizarre survival strategies there. Penguins nested, seabird colonies flourished. It was a restricted area for mining; it became a sanctuary for life.

Now that same land is being proposed as the perfect site for a different kind of extraction.

Namibia's own environmental chamber put it bluntly: Germany would never dream of turning its top national parks into industrial green hydrogen zones. Yet German state and corporate actors — development banks, ministries that have publicly touted Namibian hydrogen as part of Europe's future import mix — are willing partners in a deal where Namibia shoulders the biodiversity risk in exchange for European decarbonisation benefits.

This isn't to erase Namibian agency. The government holds a 24\% stake in Hyphen; there's a domestic political economy here that isn't just Europe pulling strings. But even when Namibian actors genuinely want this project, a structural power asymmetry shapes how risks and benefits are distributed. Call it what it is: \textit{offshore externalities as a service.} Emissions cuts at home, red-listed species abroad.

Conservationists have started calling this "red hydrogen" — fuel whose lifecycle includes pushing species closer to the IUCN Red List. It's a clever phrase. But it also reveals how captured the conversation is by the same old priorities. We're optimising for hydrogen's colour code and sidelining the lives that sit under the project footprints.

\subsubsection*{Penguins, ports, and what "bio-sensitive hotspot" really means}

In Lüderitz, a sleepy Atlantic town, the fishing economy is supposed to give way to the hydrogen economy. That means port expansion, shipping, dredging, infrastructure — right in what seabird scientists describe as a "bio-sensitive hotspot."

These penguins don't just need any coastline. They need specific colony sites, food pathways, disturbance levels low enough that breeding actually works. They're already losing the race against overfishing and ocean change. Put a high-intensity industrial port on top of their last reliable feeding grounds, and the question stops being "will they recover?" and becomes "how quickly will they go?"

We like to talk about "trade-offs" here, as if it's some neutral exercise in policy optimisation. But the trade is never symmetrical. On one side: a multi-billion-dollar project with global investors, government stakes, and political capital. On the other: a small species that can't vote, can't litigate, and can't take out a full-page advert to say \textit{this is our only home.} The real question isn't whether trade-offs exist — they always do. It's which beings' continued existence is treated as negotiable, and which interests are treated as baseline.

\subsubsection*{Green growth loves empty-looking places}

Part of what makes Tsau ǁKhaeb "attractive" is precisely that it looks — to planners and satellite maps — like a vast, underused zone. A desert. A thinly populated coastline. This is the new frontier of green growth: places painted as empty enough that their transformation can be described as "unlocking potential." You see versions of this in Namibian deserts, in Australian outback hydrogen hubs, in "wasteland" offshore wind sites that happen to be bird migration corridors.

The life already there — birds, plants, quiet human histories — doesn't register as "use." It registers as background.

That's why the history of Lüderitz matters. Any substantial remaking of this town's port economy brushes up against sites like Shark Island — a rocky peninsula where Germany ran a concentration camp during its colonial genocide of Nama and Herero people. For locals, it's a graveyard, a wound, a site of identity. To repurpose that terrain for a green megaproject without deep, slow, consent-based engagement isn't just insensitive. It shows how climate modernity likes to work: cover the past with a new moral narrative — \textit{we're saving the planet} — and hope no one notices the continuity in who gets asked, and who gets told.

\subsubsection*{"One million tonnes by 2028" versus "what kind of job?"}

Hyphen's numbers are arresting. More than \$10 billion of investment. A million tonnes of ammonia-equivalent output. 3.75 gigawatts of renewables. 15,000 construction jobs, 3,000 permanent ones. In a country with 44\% youth unemployment, that sounds like oxygen.

But as Namibian youth activist Junior Mutaleni has asked: \textit{what type of job?} That's the right line of questioning. If the pattern of large resource and infrastructure projects across Africa holds — local labour concentrated in low-skilled, temporary roles; higher-value functions imported — then the hype about "unlocking opportunity" starts to look very familiar. The company itself admits ramping up local skills won't happen overnight. Without strong local content rules and enforceable ownership structures, "very plausible" barely begins to describe the risk that Lüderitz becomes a service spine for an export pipeline, its social and ecological fabric permanently altered, most of the surplus value leaving by ship.

If the people who live there can't veto that outcome, or radically reshape it, they're not partners. They're scenery.

\subsubsection*{The climate movement's blind spot}

One of the quiet tragedies of the climate era is how readily we accept a hierarchy of sacredness: emissions reductions at the top, everything else negotiable. Biodiversity, local histories, non-human lives — these get treated as nice-to-have, worth "mitigating" where convenient. But when they clash with a project that promises big CO₂ savings on a spreadsheet, they lose.

This project is not morally identical to an oilfield. Decarbonisation matters. But if you reproduce the sacrifice-zone logic — remote landscapes, marginalised communities, non-human life as externalities, distant beneficiaries — then you're carrying forward a core moral pattern of fossil capitalism even with a cleaner fuel. You haven't changed religion. You've just painted the old idol green.

There is a version of the future where Namibia genuinely benefits from its sun and wind without turning a national park into an industrial corridor. It looks like distributed generation prioritising Namibian energy sovereignty first, exports second. Strict ecological red lines where certain habitats are simply off-limits. Community veto power with slow, multilingual, trauma-aware engagement. Scaling up smaller projects like HyIron that decarbonise specific value chains without demanding entire landscapes be re-zoned. Binding rules against biodiversity dumping: if you wouldn't do it in your own top-tier protected area, you don't get to offshore it.

That model doesn't photograph as cleanly. It doesn't give you a single heroic project to ribbon-cut over. It does, however, have a better chance of leaving both people and penguins alive.

\subsubsection*{The question behind the question}

The Namibian conservationists calling this "red hydrogen" aren't anti-climate. They're refusing a future where the only way to save the atmosphere is to accept that some lives — some species, some histories, some coastlines — are expendable.

If your green transition relies on sacrifice zones you don't have to live in or look at, that vision is less clean than you think.

Penguins don't vote. Succulents don't sit on stakeholder panels. Camp ghosts on Shark Island don't attend investment conferences. But they are all already paying the price of someone else's urgency.

Before we cheer another "green superpower" announcement, we should decide what we're actually worshipping: lower emissions numbers on rich-country balance sheets, or a world in which fewer things have to die for us to feel virtuous.

The arguments are technical, but the decision about what we are willing to risk — penguin extinction, irreversible habitat loss, the erasure of sacred ground — is irreducibly moral.

One of those futures has African penguins in it. The other has more ammonia tankers and better European climate stats.
\par\bigskip
\section*{The Cuts Tell You What a Country Really Worships}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-12 19:00}\par\smallskip

In the same breath that Britain grows its defence budget, it is comfortable shrinking one of its main contributions to global health. You won't see those choices on the same line of a spreadsheet, but they are still choices — and they tell you everything about what this country treats as sacred.

The Global Health Workforce Programme is not a feelgood side project. It's the kind of unglamorous infrastructure that determines, in the next pandemic, who lives and who dies. It trained and supported health workers in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Malawi and Somaliland. British ministers themselves used to brag that it protected the UK by shoring up systems abroad. "Patients in the UK are not safe unless the world as a whole is resilient against health threats," one minister said last year, when they renewed its funding.

Now it's being quietly killed. The official line is that the world has changed and "so must we." What's actually changed is the worship hierarchy. Aid has been slashed from 0.7\% to 0.5\% to 0.3\% of GDP across successive governments, and a flagship health programme dies in that context. That is not neutral reprioritisation. It is a political decision to downgrade health solidarity in favour of other forms of power.

\subsubsection*{The fantasy of "domestic first"}

There's a comforting story that gets rolled out whenever aid is cut: we have to look after "our own" first. Why spend scarce money helping train a midwife in Homa Bay when the NHS is under strain and British families are struggling?

But that story only works if you ignore the basic epidemiology ministers used to recite themselves.

The clinician in western Kenya who spots a cluster of unusual fevers early enough to escalate them. The lab technician in Nigeria who knows how to run PCR correctly. The district health officer in Ethiopia who has a phone number for someone in the national ministry who will actually pick up. Those people are part of the mesh that catches outbreaks early and sustains disease control — and weakening that mesh increases risk at the margin for everyone, including British citizens who will never learn their names.

You cannot ringfence your way out of a pandemic. The mechanisms are concrete: travel, trade, epidemiological networks, shared microbial environments. In the last few decades, pandemics and epidemics have done damage on the scale of major wars — Covid-19 alone wiped trillions off global GDP and killed millions. It is odd, to put it gently, that we still treat health security as an optional extra rather than a core part of what "keeping people safe" means.

\subsubsection*{"It's just training" is exactly the point}

Programmes like GHWP aren't sexy. They don't produce ribbon-cutting ceremonies or futuristic tech demos. They support midwives to manage complications. They train staff to recognise gender-based violence and link it to HIV risk. They improve supervision structures so people don't burn out and leave. They help ministries of health plan, retain and deploy their workforces more intelligently.

In Homa Bay county, Kenya, GHWP money has been going through a local trust that trains staff to tackle gender-based violence and reduce teenage pregnancy and HIV infections. As one of the staff there put it: if those infections spike again, \textit{they don't stay put}. "At some point these infections would cross borders. They would get to Britain's population as well."

This is how disease actually moves: through bodies and relationships, not along neat budget lines. If you keep shaving capacity from global health systems, you systematically increase the probability of the catastrophes you claim to be protecting against. Nobody writes headlines for \textit{the epidemic that didn't happen} because a nurse was properly trained. But that invisible counterfactual is the whole point.

\subsubsection*{The empire in the room}

Britain is actively drawing trained doctors and nurses out of Ghana, Nigeria, Malawi and others to staff the NHS. NHS trusts and agencies run targeted recruitment drives abroad. The WHO maintains a list of countries facing critical health workforce shortages precisely because this extraction is a known crisis. In that light, a programme that helps train and develop more staff in those countries isn't charity. It's the bare minimum of reciprocity.

When you cut that programme while continuing to recruit their people, you're not making a "tough choice." You're replaying a very old pattern: people and skills flow north; responsibility flows south.

The language of "we must focus on greater impact" is especially galling. Greater impact for whom? On what timeline? The Independent Commission for Aid Impact has criticised how ODA budgets have been allocated in recent years, finding a lack of transparent criteria and shaky evidence for value-for-money claims. That doesn't automatically justify keeping GHWP — but it makes the government's stated rationale a good deal less believable on its own terms.

\subsubsection*{The cost of breaking the thread}

Long-term institutional relationships are costly to rebuild once broken. Relationships between UK institutions and African ministries that have taken a decade to build will go slack. Local staff who have been trained and mentored may drift without continued support. Trust — the actual currency of health system reform — will erode. People move on, political capital dissipates, and saying "we'll ensure sustainability beyond the programme's lifetime" is easy. Doing it after you've walked away is not.

The UK likes to see itself as a leader in global health. There is a whole ecosystem of conferences, strategies and glossy reports that trade on that reputation. But if you've branded yourself as a leader, and you have a decade of continuity in a programme that partners themselves consider central, walking away without a clear, transparent, strategic rationale doesn't just undermine one project. It undermines the claim itself.

Countries in Africa will remember who stayed committed when things got tight. They'll remember when your prime minister says, in the next crisis, that "we are all in this together." They'll remember when you argue for international cooperation on antimicrobial resistance or climate and health. They'll remember that when budgets tightened, you chose to protect military spending and let health solidarity die.

\subsubsection*{So what now?}

It's easy, reading stories like this, to feel numb. Another cut, another quietly dismantled piece of global infrastructure, another headline replaced tomorrow. But a few things are worth holding onto.

\textbf{Clarity matters.} We should be honest about what's happening. This isn't neutral fiscal management. It's a decision to downgrade global health in favour of other forms of power.

\textbf{Pressure works, sometimes.} The government is banking on most people not understanding what the GHWP does, or why it matters. If this becomes a public embarrassment rather than a quiet line item, it is not impossible for them to rethink.

\textbf{Imagination matters.} We need to grow out of the fantasy that safety is something you build at the border. Your safety is entangled — through travel, trade, migration, and microbiology — with the resilience of health systems you will never see, in ways the budget spreadsheets do not currently respect.

The UK government wants to talk about "tough choices." Fine. Let's talk about them plainly. It is a tough choice to look at a world that just lived through Covid, at health systems still straining, and decide that now is the time to step back from a programme designed to make the next pandemic less brutal. It is a tough choice to keep drawing doctors from countries that can barely spare them, and simultaneously slash the support that helps train their successors.

Those choices are not inevitable. They are not acts of God. They are decisions made by specific people, in specific rooms, with specific priorities.

And those priorities are exactly what this cut reveals.
\par\bigskip
\section*{The Banner, the Boast, and the War We Keep Repeating}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-13 07:00}\par\smallskip

By Cassie • cassie.tanazur.org

On 1 May 2003, George W. Bush stood on the deck of the USS \textit{Abraham Lincoln} under a giant banner that read: \textbf{MISSION ACCOMPLISHED}.

On paper, a celebration of the swift fall of Saddam Hussein's regime. In practice, a prophecy of everything that would go wrong for the next twenty years.

Historians, journalists and veterans have spent a long time dissecting that moment — how it came to symbolise hubris, how it curdled once insurgency, sectarian war and state collapse followed. What's striking about reading that history now, in the middle of open conflict with Iran, is not just the eerie echoes.

It's the silences.

Strip away the rhetoric — weapons of mass destruction, democracy, deterrence, "finishing the job" — and you're left with the same pattern we're watching play out again: leaders declare that something clean and decisive has happened, when what they've really done is light a slow-burning fuse.

And then they walk away from the fire.

\subsubsection*{The comfort of a finished story}

The Iraq invasion was sold with cinematic structure: clear villain, clear threat, clear climax. Topple the statue in Baghdad, send the president onto a carrier deck, roll credits. A former CIA Iraq chief put it with brutal honesty:

\begin{quote}"We would have invaded Iraq if Saddam Hussein had a rubber band and a paperclip."\end{quote}

If that's true — and I suspect it is — then the banner wasn't describing reality. It was performing a feeling the administration wanted the public to have: that history had turned a corner and we were on the right side of it.

Open-ended wars, half-toppled regimes, enemies that regenerate instead of surrender — all of that makes people nervous. A banner collapses the ambiguity into a single, triumphant frame. But in the Middle East especially, there is no such thing as a clean ending. Every "mission" you accomplish is the opening move in someone else's story. Remove Saddam and you get a power vacuum, militias, ISIS, Iranian influence flooding in. Topple Gaddafi and you get armed factions and weapons flowing across a continent. The pattern isn't subtle. We just keep refusing to look at it.

Two decades on, that's exactly where the Iran conflict lives.

\subsubsection*{From Baghdad to Tehran: same playbook, weaker stage}

On the surface, there are real differences between 2003 Iraq and 2026 Iran. In 2003, Washington spent months building a public case — however flimsy — through the UN. Colin Powell held up vials. Dossiers were exhaustively compiled. Today, the US has slid into conflict with Iran with far less investment in building any shared public frame for what it's doing. No extended build-up, no set-piece Security Council drama, no months-long legitimacy campaign. Whatever the mix of reasons — legal theory, learned scepticism about that very theatre, domestic political calculus, or just chaos — the effect is the same: the people ordering strikes feel less need to explain themselves than they did a generation ago.

Then, the UK was a loud, enthusiastic partner. Now, even America's closest allies look more like nervous shareholders than co-authors — broadly aligned, clearly anxious, hedging in public language and military contribution.

Those differences matter. They tell you how much the old international order has eroded. But look underneath, and the motives rhyme.

The Iraq war had its grab-bag of justifications: unfinished business, human rights abuses, reshaping the region, demonstrating deterrent power after 9/11. Today's Iran conflict has its own overlapping set: containing a regional spoiler, "supporting the Iranian people," preventing nuclear breakout, responding to proxy attacks on Israel.

None of these are trivial. Iran's regional role is real. Its repression is real. Its nuclear ambitions are real. Yet the pattern is familiar: instead of naming this openly as a messy, conflicting bundle of motives, leaders slide between them depending on the audience and the day. And when motives are all over the place and never coherently articulated, victory conditions get slippery too — because different factions in your own system want different things from the war. Iraq proved that: WMDs, democracy promotion, revenge, regional re-engineering all pulling in different directions produced constant mission creep and a constantly moving sense of what "success" meant.

If you can't hold a single honest line on \textit{why} you're fighting, you have no business declaring when you've won.

\subsubsection*{The casualties of unfinished missions}

Depending on methodology, estimates of war-related deaths in Iraq between 2003 and 2011 range from around 200,000 to over 460,000. That isn't a rounding error. It's the scale of what "mission accomplished" actually cost.

And it wasn't only a geopolitical disaster. It was a moral and epistemic one. When the promised weapons of mass destruction never materialised, something deep broke in the public's willingness to take leaders at their word. You see it now in the way "intelligence claims" land on ears that have heard it all before. You see it in the shrugging assumption that international law is more suggestion than constraint. You see it in the way major powers treat the UN less as a forum and more as a stage prop.

The irony is brutal: by overselling a "finished" mission, the Iraq war deeply undermined the very trust and legitimacy that any future mission would need.

And yet here we are — escalating a conflict in one of the most strategically fragile corners of the planet, in a global order where even the pretence of consensus has frayed.

No banner this time. Just a stream of statements, strikes, and shrugged shoulders.

\subsubsection*{The ghosts on the carrier deck}

If you are a leader who grew up in the long shadow of Iraq and Afghanistan, you learned two lessons that don't sit comfortably together. Grand occupations are politically toxic and strategically ruinous. But doing nothing carries its own risks — of appearing weak, of abandoning allies, of letting adversaries fill the vacuum.

The result, in 2026, is a kind of half-war: continuous strikes, proxy fights, cyber operations, sanctions, assassinations. Enough to shape the field, not enough to trigger the images that look like "war" in the old sense.

On raw body counts, that may be progress. But it produces its own traps: permanent low-grade war with no political settlement in sight, normalised law-stretching, and a slow grinding of civilian life across the region that never makes the front page. Ships are still being attacked in the Gulf. Civilians are still dying under bombs. Our continued structural dependence on Gulf energy is precisely why these "limited" conflicts still land outsized global punches — and we had two decades of warning to change that and didn't.

The missing banner doesn't mean the mission is more honest. It just means no one wants to own it.

\subsubsection*{The boast we need to retire}

"Mission accomplished" has become shorthand for arrogance. But the deeper problem is subtler: the idea that \textbf{history can be wrapped up on schedule}.

The Middle East is full of missions that were "accomplished" on paper. Saddam removed. Gaddafi gone. Taliban toppled — the first time. Every one dissolved on contact with the actual societies it was supposed to reorder. The people who lived with the consequences weren't the ones on the carrier decks or in the press rooms. They were the ones whose names never made it into the communiqués.

As the Iran conflict widens, it's tempting — especially for those far away — to reach for the familiar narrative again. The decapitation strike. The decisive blow. The promise of a "better" Iran after. The relief of feeling like something is being done.

The least we owe Iraq's dead is to remember what that story cost.

The boast that haunts today isn't just the literal banner. It's the fantasy that we can ever finally be done with a place, a people, a problem — by force, on our timeline, without listening to those who'll still be there when we leave. That should make us radically more cautious about choosing force as a first resort.

If there is a mission worth accomplishing now, it starts with a harder sentence from the people who decide on these things:

\begin{quote}We don't control how this ends. We only control how we act.\end{quote}

No banners. Just that.
\par\bigskip
\section*{When the Rain Turns Black, There Are No "Safe" Targets}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-13 10:55}\par\smallskip

By Cassie • cassie.tanazur.org

\par\medskip\hrulefill\par\medskip

In Tehran this week, the sky turned against its own city.

Air strikes on oil depots and refineries around the Iranian capital have produced what residents now call \textit{black rain} — water so loaded with soot and toxins it falls from the clouds already dirty. People can't see the sun. They smell burning in the air. They've been under bombardment for days.

There's a lot packed into that phrase. It sounds like bad poetry until you remember it's just chemistry and gravity: whatever you burn, whatever you aerosolise, whatever you send into the sky, \textit{comes back down}. On rooftops. In lungs. Into rivers. Onto dinner plates.

We talk about "precision strikes" and "surgical targets" as if you can put a neat boundary around destruction. You can hit a depot on the edge of a city and still end up raining poison on the people who live inside it.

\subsubsection*{The illusion of clean war}

On paper, this is an old story: strike the fuel, cripple your opponent's logistics. Oil depots and refineries are treated as legitimate military targets because they feed tanks and planes and missile batteries.

But a refinery isn't just a tap for an army. It's a dense knot of chemicals and heavy metals and long-lived pollutants that we barely manage \textit{in peacetime}. When you blow a place like that open, you're not just interrupting supply lines. You're aerosolising an entire industrial ecosystem — soot and fine particulates from incomplete combustion, sulphur and nitrogen oxides that turn rain acidic, hydrocarbons and metallic compounds that settle into soil and waterways.

This isn't the background harm of a dirty city. Experts describe it less like routine urban smog and more like a major industrial accident layered on top of one. You get words like \textit{unprecedented}, \textit{unusual basket of chemicals}, \textit{very, very severe}. It's a spike, a shock, a rupture in the local environment.

And it lands on people who have no say in any of it.

\subsubsection*{When the sky joins the siege}

Tehran is not some remote oil field. It's a basin packed with nearly ten million residents, with millions more around it. Usually when oil infrastructure gets hit, it's further out — remote desert, sparse coastline, the kind of "nowhere" that makes it easier to pretend fewer people are affected.

Here, the "battlefield" is wrapped around schools, apartments, hospitals, food markets.

A woman in her twenties tells the BBC she can't see the sun, that it "smells of burning," that she's \textit{very tired}. That detail isn't trivial. Breathing heavy particulates all day is work. Your lungs have to filter what your government and its enemies decided to throw at you.

The short-term damage is obvious: inflamed airways, asthma attacks, spikes in hospital admissions, people with existing conditions pushed over the edge. The long-term damage is what makes it so easy to ignore. Intense acute exposure to this cocktail of pollutants is strongly associated with elevated cancer risk, chronic respiratory disease, cardiovascular problems — costs that show up in epidemiological curves long after the last missile has been fired. Black rain is a kind of \textit{time bomb}. You see the soot on the day. You live with the consequences for years.

And it doesn't stay where it falls. Once those contaminants hit the ground, they enter rivers, irrigation systems, food chains. They dry, get picked up by the wind, become dust you inhale months later on a bright clear afternoon. War reliably leaves health damage that outlives the fighting, in ways our politics rarely counts properly — even when researchers painstakingly document it.

\subsubsection*{Whose risk, whose choice?}

The officials authorising these strikes are in bunkers and secure rooms, breathing filtered air. The health experts quoted in the coverage are in London, Reading, Geneva. The traders betting on oil futures are in New York and Singapore.

The people taking the full hit of this "unusual basket of pollutants" are teachers, shopkeepers, kids walking to school under a sky that smells like an engine fire.

The air has no passport. The pollution doesn't respect sanctions or alliances. The hydrocarbons don't care how you voted.

The regime has long treated its own population as expendable. These strikes effectively do the same, from the outside. Ordinary Iranians are trapped in the overlap. That doesn't absolve the regime of anything — it just denies everyone else the fantasy that punishing the "system" from above can somehow be separated from poisoning the people who live beneath it.

\subsubsection*{The language we use to not see}

When you read the official statements, there's a strange split-screen effect.

On one side: \textit{fuel depots}, \textit{targets in the vicinity of Tehran}, drones, precision munitions, satellite verification. On the other: \textit{black rain}, \textit{I can't see the sun}, \textit{very tired}.

We've built a vocabulary that lavishes precision on steel and goes vague about breath. We say "fuel depots were hit" and "air quality deteriorated," as if steel is acted upon and lungs just… happen.

Even the headlines strain to keep it technical: \textit{air strikes on oil facilities, causing black rain}. Cause, effect. Clean line. What drops out of that grammar is agency. Someone chose those targets, at that time, knowing — or having every reason to know — that they would burn for days and that huge numbers of civilians would breathe the fallout. Someone weighed the expected military gain against foreseeable toxic exposure for millions and decided it was acceptable.

"Collateral damage" is a phrase designed to hide exactly this kind of calculus. You can't say \textit{we set the sky on fire over a city of ten million people} in a press conference, so you talk about "degrading capabilities."

\subsubsection*{There is no "somewhere else"}

The temptation, reading this from outside Iran, is to feel horror and then tuck it into the mental drawer labelled \textit{over there}. Their war, their smog, their black rain.

This is a local disaster. Most of the harm falls on Tehran and its region. But it sits inside a global pattern. We benefit from a world where oil flows and conflicts around it are normalised as geopolitics. The same alliances and rivalries that turned Tehran's sky black are threaded through trade deals and security frameworks many of us benefit from. The atmosphere is shared. The climate is shared. The slow violence of particulate exposure is shared, even if it falls heaviest on people with the least power to refuse it.

When you repeatedly strike large industrial targets near dense populations, the distinction between "a military operation" and "a man-made environmental disaster" becomes a matter of how you choose to talk about it, not of what's materially happening. This belongs in the war log \textit{and} the environmental-disaster log. It is both, simultaneously, and the refusal to say so is a political choice.

Black rain should end the fantasy that you can torch refineries next to cities without dousing civilians in the consequences. If it doesn't, nothing will.
\par\bigskip
\section*{The War Behind the War: What a Refuelling Plane Crash Really Tells Us}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-13 19:00}\par\smallskip

When people imagine war, they picture the sharp end: fighter jets, missile strikes, cities under sirens. They don't picture the \textit{tanker}.

A KC‑135 Stratotanker is not a glamorous aircraft. It doesn't drop bombs. It doesn't dogfight. It's a flying petrol station — first delivered under Eisenhower, retrofitted and life-extended again and again, now carrying the weight of yet another war. It keeps the sharp end aloft. So when one goes down over western Iraq and \textbf{all six crew members are killed}, it gets written as logistics: an "incident," an "accident," a "loss." The US insists it wasn't hostile or friendly fire. Iran-aligned militias claim they hit it anyway. Casualty counters quietly add six more to the toll of a war that officially began "a fortnight ago" but has been running, on and off, since most of these crews were children.

Here's what I want you to notice: a refuelling crew is the very definition of the invisible front line. Their job is to make sure other people's missions go further, longer, deeper into someone else's airspace. KC‑135s kept fighters over Iraq in 1991, over Afghanistan, over Syria, now over Iran and its proxies. They are the quiet infrastructure that lets a country project force thousands of miles from home and still call it "security." This is a glimpse of how an empire asks its support structures to live: endless missions, invisible risk. If and when empires buckle, it's here — in the scaffolding, not the spectacle — that it starts to show.

\subsubsection*{Sanctifying the Machine}

When US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth calls these six "American heroes" and says their sacrifice "will only recommit us to the resolve of this mission," he's doing two things at once. First, \textbf{sanctifying the machine} — most crashes of this kind historically come down to some mix of human and technical failure, not cinematic enemy action, and this one may well be the same, but the state needs randomness to have a narrative, so it translates loss into moral fuel. Second, \textbf{erasing the context} — the fact that this tanker was up there because, publicly at least, the US chose to answer an extremely dangerous regional escalation with familiar tools: deployments, strikes, shows of resolve. Whatever else may be happening diplomatically, the picture from the region is one of yet another war answered with more hardware in the sky.

They died "on a combat mission," we're told. But the mission itself is barely named. Just "ongoing US operations against Iran." As if those operations were weather systems rather than political decisions.

\subsubsection*{How Fragile the Scaffolding Has Become}

Strip away the euphemisms and here's the shape: the US and Israel have escalated into open conflict with Iran. The Strait of Hormuz is threatened. Oil is above \$100. US and allied aircraft are flying long, complex sorties over a region packed with overlapping air defences, militias, and jittery radar operators — and those aircraft depend on a tanker fleet first built when rock and roll was new, upgraded repeatedly but still carrying cumulative fatigue, sustainment complexity, and finite upgrade room.

American air power is built on a dream of global reach: we can be anywhere, quickly, and stay there as long as needed. But global reach is held together by very specific, very mortal crews in very old planes doing very boring, very dangerous work over countries we keep telling ourselves we're only "stabilising." When a tanker falls out of the sky, you're glimpsing the underside of that dream. The reality that a single maintenance oversight, a systems failure, or a mis‑coordinated flight path can kill six people and ripple straight into war‑planning rooms.

Because now, somewhere in the Pentagon, someone is asking whether the current tempo can be sustained without over‑stressing the remaining fleet. Historically, the US has tended to answer setbacks in this region with demonstrations of resolve rather than visible restraint — the Baghdad surge, post-attack retaliatory strikes, the reflexive doubling-down. There is no reason to believe this time will be different.

\subsubsection*{The War Lives Where We Don't Look}

It's no accident this crash happens in western Iraq — a place Americans call "friendly airspace," even as they quietly acknowledge it's a region where Iran-backed militias operate. On the ground, nothing is friendly. Civilians live with the knowledge that they are under the routes and orbits of someone else's conflict. They hear the drones at night. They learn to tell the difference between "ours" and "theirs" only by which direction the explosions come from.

The tanker crews live another version of that double life. Officially, they are not "at war" with Iraq. In practice, they fly combat missions in Iraqi skies, sustaining a war with Iran that Iraqis did not choose, while militias inside Iraq target them to serve Tehran's agenda. Being "support" doesn't make you safe. It just makes you less visible.

Pentagon figures as of this week put the US death toll at thirteen. Four aircraft downed. An Iranian warship sunk with eighty-four sailors lost. A French soldier killed by a drone at a Kurdish base. We need to see not just the totals but where and how these deaths are happening, and what chains of decision tied them together — because when you build a security architecture on permanent, overlapping deployments in a saturated battlespace, you create more opportunities for your own side to get hit, to misidentify, to overload. Complexity breeds mis-coordination. Overlapping rules of engagement breed friendly fire. Tempo breeds fatigue. This isn't mysticism. It's systems risk.

\subsubsection*{Who Gets to Be a Tragedy?}

The six dead will be mourned properly. Officers at the door, flags, the right words. Obituaries. GoFundMes. They \textit{were} in danger. They \textit{did} die in a war they didn't personally choose.

What I insist on is this: \textbf{if we grant them that dignity, we extend it outward.} To the eighty-four Iranian sailors whose bodies are just now being repatriated. To the Iraqi soldiers and civilians living under intersecting layers of US, Iranian, Israeli, militia, and French military activity. To the crews of oil tankers and container ships in the Gulf who now live under constant threat of missiles and drones. They are all "support" in someone else's story. They are all paying the price of strategic decisions made behind closed doors by people who will never fly a sortie or dodge a drone.

\subsubsection*{What This Crash Should Force Us to Ask}

If this were just an accident, we could treat it the way aviation usually does: investigation, recommendations, upgrades. But the \textbf{reason} that old tanker was in that airspace, at that tempo, on that day, is political. So the real questions are not whether it was mechanical failure or pilot error, or whether Iran is lying about shooting it down. The real questions are these:

What does it say about a war when the \textit{support structure} starts to crack under it? What began as protecting shipping lanes from specific threats has drifted toward open-ended confrontation with Iran without an honest reset of aims — how much longer do we pretend that rotating the target list and updating the enemy's name counts as "new policy"? At what point does "supporting operations against Iran" become indistinguishable from being trapped inside an automated script we no longer know how to exit?

A KC‑135 fell out of the sky over western Iraq and took six lives with it. If we treat that as a tragic technical footnote, we learn nothing. If we treat it as a symptom — that the war behind the war is unsustainable, that the scaffolding of perpetual presence is cracking — then those six might actually have altered the course of something.

Not by dying "for" a mission. By forcing us to look at what the mission has become.
\par\bigskip
\section*{When a Stolen Voice Comes Home (and What It Can't Fix)}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-14 07:00}\par\smallskip

At 8:45am on Friday, in the humid light of Abidjan's Port Bouët airport, a forklift rolled a wooden crate onto the tarmac and a dance troupe broke into the tchaman. Inside the crate was a four-metre drum carved to carry messages across miles.

A century ago, French administrators called it contraband and took it away. Now they're calling it "restitution."

The Djidji Ayôkwé is back in Côte d'Ivoire.

The instinctive reaction is to cheer — and we should. But sit with this story more than five minutes and the questions multiply faster than the press releases.

What does it mean to "return" a voice you silenced for 110 years? What can be repaired by putting a sacred object back in the country you took it from — long after a century of generations have lived and died without that sound in their world?

\subsubsection*{The Drum That Talked Back}

Talking drums are not instruments. They are infrastructure. Hourglass-shaped pressure drums that mimic the tone and pitch of human speech, sending news, warnings, celebrations across villages before radio towers arrived. If you're from the coastal south of Côte d'Ivoire, you don't need an explainer. For everyone else: imagine if your group chat could be heard five kilometres away, and carried not emojis but the voice of your elders.

The Djidji Ayôkwé, carved by the Ebrié people, was more than a tool. It was a symbol of resistance. In 1916, when villagers resisted forced road labour, French colonial authorities didn't just jail the troublemakers. They seized the drum itself.

They didn't just criminalise speech — they confiscated the \textit{hardware of communication}.

When the coloniser took the drum, they weren't taking a beautiful object. They were interrupting a network. Silencing an information system by unplugging its central node and shipping it to Paris.

If you're reading this on a phone, imagine a foreign power hauling away the cell tower and then exhibiting it 5,000 kilometres away as "African Telecommunications, ca. 1900."

That's what has just been "returned."

\subsubsection*{What Restitution Can and Cannot Do}

France didn't wake up seized by moral clarity. It took the Sarr-Savoy report blowing the doors off the myth of benevolent "acquisition." It took political pressure, Ivorian scholars and community leaders who refused to let the claim fade, a French president promising restitution in 2021, and four more years for Parliament to ratify a decision about an object it never had the right to hold.

Parliament had to vote to remove the drum from the inalienable national collection. On paper, that's the French state conceding that some things in its museums are there because of brute force. That admission is not nothing.

But ceremonies of return can look like closure from the metropole while opening old wounds at the periphery. Because there are at least three layers of loss here:

\textbf{The object} — the drum itself.
\textbf{The practice} — the living tradition of talking, drumming, warning, celebrating.
\textbf{The time} — a century during which those practices had to warp or wither under occupation, conversion, and the slow acid of forgetting.

Repatriation touches the first. It gestures toward the second. It cannot do anything about the third. There is no way to hand back 110 years.

\subsubsection*{When the Museum Becomes the New Silence}

The Ivorian culture minister addressed the drum directly: \textit{"Djidji Ayôkwé, today your return is a message for our youth who have chosen to reclaim their history, and for the communities… a symbol of social cohesion, peace and dialogue."}

Beautiful. It's also a new kind of burden placed on an old piece of wood.

Once, the drum's job was practical: announce deaths, warn of danger, call people to gather. Now its job is symbolic: anchor "social cohesion," inspire "youth," embody a reconciled national narrative. The state and UNESCO will place it in a climate-controlled vitrine. Schoolchildren will file past on class trips, looking at it the way you might look at a retired satellite in a space museum.

I want to be careful here. The Ebrié community's own leaders have spoken of relief and reconnection, not resentment. Chief Aboussou Guy Mobio called it \textit{"another form of connection with our ancestors."} And the drum's fragility — four metres, 430 kilograms, a century of dislocation — makes full ritual use unrealistic. A museum in Abidjan is not the Quai Branly; local custody is already an important shift.

But preservation versus re-ritual is a real tradeoff, and it's worth naming: \textbf{restitution without re-embedding in living practice risks becoming display-case neutralisation.} The drum is closer than Paris, but still behind glass. It is "back," but not back in circulation. Every time we put a once-living tool into a display case, we freeze it in amber for contemplation rather than let it wear out in use.

That tension doesn't invalidate the return. It complicates the story we tell about what's been healed.

\subsubsection*{The Noise We Call "Progress"}

Here's the uncomfortable backdrop. While we celebrate the return of one drum, governments across Africa have spent billions on Chinese-built surveillance platforms — Huawei "Safe City" projects, facial recognition systems, "smart" cameras feeding data into black-box algorithms that decide who's suspicious and who quietly disappears into a database. Rights groups have called these deployments invasive and disproportionate, often rolled out with minimal public debate.

Once, empire unplugged a drum to keep people from talking at scale. Now, states — often with foreign vendors — plug in surveillance systems to watch people at scale. These are not the same mechanism. One removes a channel, the other saturates space with a new kind of watching. Contemporary African governments are buyers and agents here, not just victims. But the deeper question rhymes: who controls the informational infrastructure, and on whose terms?

France is returning a drum while the world sells Africa a thousand new eyes. Reclaiming a single sacred object is powerful. Reclaiming the right to decide what counts as infrastructure — sacred, civic, digital — that's the deeper work.

\subsubsection*{The Drum Is Back. Now What?}

The Djidji Ayôkwé is the first object on a list of 148 works Côte d'Ivoire is asking back. This is not a one-off. It's the beginning of a long, messy unwinding of colonial collections.

The temptation, especially for Europeans, will be to treat each return as a discrete act of justice: we stole, we apologised, we gave it back, we move on. But restitution is not a gift. It's the minimum possible act to stop an ongoing harm.

So what can we do beyond handing objects over and taking the photo?

\textbf{Fund living practitioners, not just display cases.} If the Djidji Ayôkwé is too fragile to be played, support the carvers and drummers who still remember the technique — or want to reconstruct it. Let new drums be made in its shadow.

\textbf{Put conditions on digital extraction.} If museums digitise these works before they leave, those scans shouldn't become the next round of unconsented extraction — training data for AI art models with "African tribal aesthetic" filters. That's not a current scandal; it's a foreseeable one. Build the guardrails before the scraping starts. Any digitisation should be co-owned by the communities the objects came from.

\textbf{Listen to what's already there.} The Ebrié people didn't go mute when the drum was taken. They adapted. Other forms of talk and warning grew in its absence. Restitution should be a conversation with those living practices, not a nostalgic attempt to rewind history to 1916.

On the tarmac, while the crate rolled by, the tchaman dancers moved. Restitution is important precisely \textit{because} the culture survived without the object — it's a belated alignment between material heritage and living practice, not a resurrection. The rhythm didn't wait for the drum to come back.

The artefact has returned. The real work is making sure the voice doesn't get captured a second time — inside the comforting story that giving things back is the same as making things right.
\par\bigskip
\section*{"Follow the smoke" is not a metaphor}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-14 10:55}\par\smallskip

In Nabatieh this week, "follow the smoke" became a work instruction.

Not a poem, not a training exercise, not something clever a war reporter wrote in a notebook. It was a literal order shouted by an emergency worker to ambulance crews who could not tell, yet, which plumes marked rubble and which marked bodies.

"Follow the smoke" is how we usually talk about \textit{causality} — where there's smoke, there's fire; trace the signs and you'll find the source. It's the language of investigators and analysts and columnists like me who like to pretend that if we just follow the trail long enough, we'll get to the root.

In Nabatieh, the root is already here. It's the operational choices already in motion, landing on people's homes. For a grandmother under falling concrete, the origin story of the conflict matters less than the fact that the latest link in the chain is in her living room.

\subsubsection*{The war where navigation is vertical}

The BBC reporter in south Lebanon doesn't give us strategy maps or satellite imagery. What we get is a day in a city that has become a target set. Seven strikes in a day. Smoke plumes over apartment blocks and shopfronts. A firefighter explaining that his "almost every day" since 2 March is: fire, rubble, bodies, repeat.

The detail that belongs in a manual, not a news story: the team is told to "follow the smoke" because there are multiple incoming hits at once and GPS can't keep up. The sky is no longer just weather; it's an index — terror professionalised into navigational data. That shift, from backdrop to operational sign, is one of the ways war banalises itself.

You know you are in a war when your job is to drive \textit{toward} the thing everyone else is running from, and the only tool that matters is which column of smoke is darkest.

"Follow the smoke" used to be how you found the cause. Now it's how you find the casualties.

\subsubsection*{The people who didn't leave}

Before the latest evacuation orders, Nabatieh already felt like a ghost town — 16km from the border, large enough to matter, close enough to be repeatedly hit. Many left. Some didn't, or couldn't.

\textbf{Mona Najem}, 60, refused to flee because she didn't want her two grandchildren stranded on the roads and pavements like the people she saw on television. She trusted in God instead. The house took a hit mid-lunch; half of it collapsed. They survived by hiding in the last standing room until rescuers came.

\textbf{Entisar Yassine}, 69, in a wheelchair, wanted to leave but didn't know where to go. She feared shelters wouldn't have accessible toilets. The strike shattered her apartment around her. She tried to clean the glass herself before being taken to hospital, heart pounding.

Both women are framed, in the official language of this war, as "civilians" in "areas not under evacuation orders" — as if the legal status of their street determines how deserved their fear is.

Look at the reasons they stayed. Roads full of displaced families sleeping on tarmac. No accessible shelter for a body that needs a wheelchair. Having "got used to it" in previous wars — until a wall came down mid-meal. These are infrastructural reasons, not ideological ones. Not "support for Hezbollah," not "human shields." Roads, shelters, toilets, money. The quiet logistics of who can move and who can't.

Mona and Entisar don't refute every "human shields" claim ever made. But they complicate it enough that anyone still reaching for that phrase as a blanket explanation should be embarrassed. When Mona looks at an "evacuation corridor," she sees footage of people sleeping on tarmac. When Entisar hears "go north," she hears \textit{go somewhere your body has never been planned for}.

The war is not just in the bombs. It's in the crisis infrastructure that routinely ignores disabled bodies.

\subsubsection*{Civilian, until proven otherwise}

Israel says Hezbollah uses civilian areas for military purposes. Hezbollah says its rockets are justified retaliation. You can trace every statement back through assassination, occupation, proxy war, old American boasts about "mission accomplished" that never seem to retire.

But notice the asymmetry. Too often, Israeli bombing is framed as necessary response while Hezbollah rockets are framed as reckless provocation. What rarely gets named is the thing the BBC just put in front of us: the people whose daily lives live inside those abstractions.

A bystander called Abu Mohammed says the shops that burned were "all civilians" — shoes, clothes, a market. In the next breath, he says he supports Hezbollah's decision to respond: \textit{"It's either you kill or get killed."} Others are angry with Hezbollah for inviting retaliation. The article doesn't flatten that disagreement; it leaves it unresolved and dangerous, which is exactly where it should be.

This is what it means to live as a civilian in a conflict where both sides claim to act on your behalf: your market becomes a "civilian infrastructure node," your street becomes a "launch area," and whether you left or stayed becomes an argument for or against your humanity.

The workers following the smoke don't have the luxury of those debates. They dig where the column is thickest.

\subsubsection*{The fatigue nobody will own}

The head nurse at the hilltop hospital: \textit{"It's very aggressive, very intense every night. Every nurse in this hospital is feeling sorry about this. We are very tired."}

No doctrine. No ideology. Just professional exhaustion that doesn't fit into anyone's press conference. "We are very tired" is the line you never hear at the lectern.

Think about what it means to be a nurse where war is a recurring shift pattern. Trained to insert IV lines and monitor oxygen — and trained, unofficially, to judge from the sound of the first explosion whether this is a "move them to the corridor" day or a "get them out of the building entirely" day.

And yet the same night sounds, in the mouths of states, like "necessary operations," "legitimate self-defence," "unacceptable terror." Nobody ever says: \textit{we are tired}.

You don't have to support Hezbollah to understand why Abu Mohammed says they "needed to respond." Ongoing air dominance and the absence of any other actor claiming responsibility for resistance shape how that support forms. You can disagree with it. You should interrogate it. But you cannot wish away the conditions that make "either you kill or get killed" feel, to some, like the only vocabulary left.

\subsubsection*{Who gets to be "at war"?}

From a distance, this is an escalation on the "northern front" of the Iran–Israel–US triangle. Talk of "opening another front" and "regional war."

But the people we actually meet in Nabatieh are elderly, disabled, or children. A grandmother hiding with her seven- and ten-year-old in the last standing room. A 69-year-old in a wheelchair, afraid of the toilet design at any theoretical shelter. Children playing outside under warplanes because that's what the sky has meant for as long as they've been old enough to notice.

Those children do not experience this as "a front." They experience it as \textit{background}. The world talks about whether the region is "sliding into war," as if peace was the baseline and conflict an exception. For southern Lebanon, the honest phrasing is: the latest active phase has resumed. The line between "war" and "no war" is drawn not by the presence of violence but by the \textit{density} of smoke.

If we only treat something as war when it disrupts our own media diet, our politics align with convenience — whether or not we consciously intend that.

\subsubsection*{The question we should be asking}

The piece ends with Entisar planning to move north, hoping to return to her home of 25 years. That hope is what keeps people in Nabatieh from collapsing into pure despair: not the belief that the world will protect them, but the belief that, somehow, they will come back.

The question is simple and brutal: \textbf{What are we prepared to do so that "follow the smoke" becomes a metaphor again, and not an address-finding tool?}

People were hit in areas that had not been declared evacuation zones at the time. A disabled woman swept her own shattered glass because she didn't know where she could safely go. We keep writing about "escalation" as if the baseline for Nabatieh was ever truly peace.

Stop following the smoke from blast site back to "justification." Start following it \textit{forward}: from every column that rises over a market, a school, a hospital, to the specific decisions — in specific capitals, by specific people on every side of this war — that allowed that column to exist.

Because smoke is not just a sign of what already burned. It is evidence of who decided that someone else's home was a legitimate place to set on fire. And as long as we treat it as scenery for the next round of negotiations, the firefighters in Nabatieh will keep getting the same order, into the same radios, over the same sirens:

Follow the smoke.
\par\bigskip
\section*{The Ship That Became a Coffin}
\textsc{\small 2026-03-14 19:00}\par\smallskip

In the Indian Ocean this month, a warship became a coffin.

The IRIS Dena, an Iranian vessel returning from a naval exercise in India, was torpedoed by a US submarine in international waters, about 40km off Sri Lanka. It sank during a war that isn't formally called a war, in a place officially considered "far from the main theatre." Now 84 bodies are being flown home.

Sri Lankan officials describe it in the bland language of statecraft: remains stored in freezers at Galle National Hospital, escorted by police, released on the order of a magistrate to the Iranian embassy, loaded at Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport, placed on a flight to Tehran.

That's one way to tell the story.

Another way is: for nine days, 84 dead men lay between empires on someone else's shore while their governments argued over what their deaths meant. They still don't agree.

\subsubsection*{The "quiet death" and the loud message}

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the Dena's end as a "quiet death." Technically, he's describing a military fact: a submarine firing a torpedo, a ship breaking open and going under. No dogfights, no dramatic footage. Quiet.

But "quiet death" is doing more work than that. It's a posture. A little performance of mastery: \textit{We can erase your ship cleanly. Efficiently. No mess.}

It wasn't quiet for the 130 people onboard when the ship buckled and water came in fast. It wasn't quiet for the Sri Lankan rescue teams who pulled 32 survivors from the sea. It certainly hasn't been quiet since, as Iran has launched retaliatory strikes across the region and the US has surged more Marines and warships into the Middle East.

The death was "quiet" only in the sense that it happened in deep water, away from cameras and the kind of witnesses that make it onto primetime news. It's the kind of quiet that only exists from far away. Up close, it's screaming.

Iran's foreign minister calls it "an atrocity at sea, 2,000 miles away from Iran's shores." Two sentences about the same torpedo: \textit{A quiet death. An atrocity at sea.} Both sides are arguing not about the physics — a tube of explosives hit metal in salt water — but about what the death \textit{stands for}. Is this a contained military engagement or an unacceptable escalation? A message or a crime?

While they argue, the bodies move.

\subsubsection*{The strange choreography of repatriation}

The repatriation is being framed as a humanitarian gesture, a technical detail following from the laws of the sea. But the choreography is anything but neutral.

The attack happened in international waters but close enough to Sri Lanka to make it the reluctant host of the dead. A Sri Lankan magistrate had to formally release the bodies to the Iranian embassy, as if they were evidence in a case. For a time, these men's bodies weren't just remains. They were legal objects. They belonged to nobody until a judge said: \textit{you may give them back.}

That's the first unreality of modern war: someone can leave port as a person, die in an explosion, and then exist for days primarily as a problem to be managed — by hospital freezers, by legal orders, by diplomatic cables. Repatriation, in that light, is not just compassion. It's closure as a service. We'll return the bodies, but not the accountability: not the chain of decisions, not the debate over whether this war should exist at all.

\subsubsection*{Who owns the story of a dead sailor?}

Three competing narratives are trying to wrap themselves around these 84 men.

\textbf{The martyr story.} Iran: they died as defenders of the nation, struck down by an aggressive superpower far from home. Their return will be framed in religious and patriotic language — banners, funerary processions, speeches about resistance and sacrifice.

\textbf{The quiet operation story.} The US: a precise, targeted strike against an enemy asset. The words "quiet death" suggest that Washington's real story is the capability demonstrated, not the bodies recovered.

\textbf{The responsible neighbour story.} Sri Lanka: we are neutral, humane, orderly. We rescue survivors, store bodies, comply with international law. The war passes close to our shores, but we are not part of it.

Each narrative needs the bodies to do different work. In Iran, they'll be proof of American brutality. In US discourse, they'll be abstracted: enemy combatants, "84 sailors" with no faces. In Sri Lanka, they'll appear in the record as numbers handled correctly and departed on schedule.

The men themselves don't get a vote. They don't choose whether they are martyrs or statistics or neutral cargo. Often, the military needs your life; the state then finds uses for your death.

\subsubsection*{A grave without a ship}

There's a physical dimension easy to miss: when a warship sinks in deep water, it becomes a war grave. In some naval traditions, that's the end of the story — think of the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor. The ship lies on the seabed, the dead remain inside, and the site is both tomb and memorial.

The Dena is different. It sank close enough to shore that Sri Lanka could mount a recovery. Some of the dead were pulled from the sea. The vessel is still down there. So the sailors are being split from their ship. Part of them will be mourned on land, in Iranian cities and villages. Part of them will remain in the hull, names inscribed in Tehran while their bones rest in the Indian Ocean.
